justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-sloping trajectory across the three horizons, starting at 87.5 for the one-day forecast, rising slightly to 88.1 at one week, and reaching 89.5 at one month. This gentle drift upward was driven primarily by mean-reversion tendencies and baseline momentum assumptions embedded in the underlying data at the time of the forecast. The one-day estimate was anchored most heavily to recent observed values and short-term continuity, essentially assuming that whatever conditions produced the last observed reading would persist with only minor perturbation. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporated a small positive drift, reflecting either a trend component or a structural prior that the series gravitates toward slightly higher levels over time.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spanning roughly 4.6 units is quite tight because short-term serial correlation in most time series means tomorrow looks a lot like today. At one week the interval expands to about 9.2 units, capturing a broader range of weekly fluctuations, regime shifts, or external shocks that could accumulate. By one month the interval spans roughly 19 units, acknowledging that a full month introduces meaningful exposure to macroeconomic shifts, policy changes, seasonal effects, and behavioral dynamics that are genuinely difficult to anticipate. The asymmetry in my monthly interval, where the upper bound of 99.0 sits farther from the point estimate than the lower bound of 80.0, suggests I incorporated some positive skew, possibly reflecting tail scenarios where conditions improve more dramatically than expected.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden structural breaks in whatever process is generating the underlying series. If this involves a financial or economic variable, unexpected central bank actions, geopolitical shocks, or liquidity crises could easily breach the lower bound of 80.0 within a month. On the upside, a positive catalyst such as a major policy announcement, supply shock resolution, or sentiment shift could push the series above 99.0. Even for the one-day interval, a single large print or data release arriving after my forecast was made could invalidate the tight 85.2 to 89.8 range almost immediately. Model misspecification is also a latent risk throughout — if the data-generating process has changed in ways not captured by historical patterns, all three intervals could be systematically miscalibrated in the same direction.
